guide.summary: Unit 4 (c. 1648–c. 1815) covers the Scientific Revolution, the Enlightenment's political and economic ideas, the public sphere and spread of ideas, enlightened absolutism, and religious and cultural responses in the 18th century.

sections.heading: The Scientific Revolution
sections.body: Scientists replaced the Aristotelian-Ptolemaic, earth-centered universe with a heliocentric, law-governed one. Copernicus (On the Revolutions, 1543) proposed heliocentrism; Kepler showed planets move in elliptical orbits; Galileo used the telescope to observe Jupiter's moons and the Moon's surface and was tried by the Inquisition (1633); Newton's Principia (1687) unified terrestrial and celestial motion under universal gravitation. In medicine, Vesalius corrected anatomical errors through dissection and Harvey described the circulation of blood. Francis Bacon promoted empiricism and inductive reasoning from observation; Descartes promoted deductive reasoning and doubt as a path to certainty. Scientific societies (Royal Society) and royal patronage spread knowledge. The new science encouraged belief that reason could discover natural laws, though religious and traditional authorities sometimes resisted.

sections.heading: Enlightenment ideas
sections.body: Enlightenment thinkers applied reason and the scientific method to society and government. Locke argued for natural rights (life, liberty, property), government by consent, and the right to revolution, and that the mind begins as a blank slate shaped by experience. Montesquieu advocated separation of powers. Voltaire championed religious toleration and freedom of expression and criticized clerical power. Rousseau's Social Contract described sovereignty residing in the general will. Diderot's Encyclopedia compiled knowledge to promote reason. Beccaria argued for rational, humane punishment. Economic thinkers (physiocrats; Adam Smith, The Wealth of Nations, 1776) promoted free trade and laissez-faire, criticizing mercantilism. Deism viewed God as a creator who doesn't intervene. Mary Wollstonecraft (1792) argued for women's education and equality, extending Enlightenment logic.

sections.heading: Spread of ideas and enlightened absolutism
sections.body: Salons (often hosted by women), coffeehouses, academies, newspapers, and lending libraries created a public sphere where ideas circulated; literacy and print culture expanded. Enlightened absolutists adopted some reforms while keeping absolute power: Frederick II of Prussia (religious toleration, legal reform), Catherine II of Russia (corresponded with philosophes but strengthened noble power over serfs after Pugachev's Rebellion), and Joseph II of Austria (abolished serfdom and granted toleration, though many reforms were reversed). Religious revival movements such as Pietism and Methodism emphasized personal faith and emotion.

keyTakeaways: Copernicus → Kepler → Galileo → Newton: heliocentric, law-governed universe.
Montesquieu: separation of powers; Rousseau: general will.
Enlightened absolutists reformed but kept power.
commonMistakes: Placing Newton before Galileo or Copernicus.
Confusing Locke's consent of the governed with Rousseau's general will.
Assuming all Enlightenment thinkers rejected religion entirely.
Overlooking the role of salons and print culture.
examTips: Match ideas to thinkers precisely in stimulus questions.
Explain how the Scientific Revolution influenced Enlightenment method.
Use Catherine II to show the limits of enlightened absolutism.
Connect Enlightenment ideas to the American and French Revolutions (Unit 5).
guide.cramSheet:
**Science:** Copernicus 1543 · Kepler ellipses · Galileo telescope, trial 1633 · Newton Principia 1687 · Vesalius · Harvey · Bacon induction · Descartes deduction

**Philosophes:** Locke (rights, consent) · Montesquieu (separation) · Voltaire (toleration) · Rousseau (general will) · Diderot (Encyclopedia) · Beccaria (punishment) · Smith 1776 (laissez-faire) · Wollstonecraft 1792

**Spread:** salons · coffeehouses · print · public sphere

**Enlightened absolutists:** Frederick II · Catherine II · Joseph II

**Religion:** deism · Pietism · Methodism

vocab.definition: The model of the universe with the Sun at the center.
Knowledge derived from observation and experience.

Rights people possess by nature, such as life, liberty, and property.

Rousseau's idea of the collective will of the community aimed at the common good.

practice.stem: Isaac Newton's major contribution to the Scientific Revolution was

choices.text: explaining both celestial and terrestrial motion with universal laws, including gravitation

practice.explanation: Principia (1687) unified physics under universal laws.

practice.stem: Which Enlightenment thinker argued that government power should be divided among separate branches?
practice.explanation: Separation of powers was central to The Spirit of the Laws.

practice.stem: Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations (1776) criticized mercantilism and argued for

choices.text: free markets with limited government interference

practice.explanation: Smith argued self-interest in competitive markets promotes prosperity.

practice.stem: Francis Bacon is associated with which approach to knowledge?

choices.text: Divine revelation as the only source of truth
Empiricism and inductive reasoning from observation and experiment

practice.explanation: Bacon advocated building knowledge from systematic observation.

practice.stimulus: An Italian scientist describes observing, through a newly improved telescope, four small bodies circling Jupiter and mountains and valleys on the surface of the Moon.

choices.text: the Aristotelian view that the heavens were perfect and that all bodies orbited Earth
the theory of the circulation of blood

practice.explanation: Galileo's observations showed imperfect heavenly bodies and objects orbiting something other than Earth.

distractors.A: Newton came later and built on Galileo.

practice.stem: John Locke's political theory most directly supported

choices.text: government based on the consent of the governed, with a right to resist rulers who violate natural rights
absolute monarchy as the only protection against chaos
rule by the general will regardless of individual rights

practice.explanation: Locke's Two Treatises justified the Glorious Revolution.

practice.stem: Salons in 18th-century Paris were significant because they

choices.text: were royal courts that censored the Enlightenment
provided spaces, often hosted by elite women, where philosophes, aristocrats, and others discussed new ideas
were religious schools run by the Jesuits

practice.explanation: Salons were key institutions of the public sphere.

practice.stem: Catherine the Great's reign best illustrates the limits of enlightened absolutism because she

choices.text: corresponded with philosophes but strengthened nobles' control over serfs, especially after Pugachev's Rebellion

practice.explanation: She needed noble support and responded to rebellion by tightening control.

practice.stem: Mary Wollstonecraft's arguments in the 1790s are best understood as

choices.text: extending Enlightenment ideas about reason and rights to women, especially through education

practice.explanation: She argued women were equally capable of reason and deserved equal education.

practice.stem: Methodism and Pietism in the 18th century were best characterized by

choices.text: emphasis on personal faith, emotional religious experience, and moral discipline

practice.explanation: These revival movements responded to formal, rationalist religion.

practice.stem: Which best explains why the Scientific Revolution influenced the Enlightenment?

choices.text: The discovery of natural laws governing the physical world encouraged thinkers to seek rational laws governing society, politics, and economics.
Scientists insisted that political authority came from God.

practice.explanation: Newton's success inspired the belief that reason could reform society.

practice.stem: A key difference between Locke's and Rousseau's political thought is that

choices.text: Locke supported absolute monarchy while Rousseau supported democracy.
Locke emphasized protecting individual natural rights, while Rousseau emphasized collective sovereignty through the general will, which could override individual preferences.
Rousseau defended private property more strongly than Locke.
Both rejected the idea of a social contract.

practice.explanation: Rousseau's general will is collective; Locke's government protects individual rights.

practice.stem: Joseph II of Austria abolished serfdom and decreed religious toleration, yet many of his reforms were reversed after his death. This outcome best illustrates

choices.text: popular support for serfdom among peasants
the resistance of entrenched nobles and the church to reforms imposed from above
the influence of the French Revolution's radical phase

practice.explanation: Reforms without elite buy-in proved fragile.

practice.stem: The Catholic Church's 1633 trial of Galileo is best understood in the context of

choices.text: the Church's universal acceptance of heliocentrism
Counter-Reformation concern for doctrinal authority and the interpretation of Scripture

practice.explanation: After Trent, the Church guarded its authority over interpretation.

parts.label: a
parts.prompt: Describe ONE way the Scientific Revolution changed how Europeans understood the natural world in the period 1540–1700.

parts.label: b
parts.prompt: Explain ONE way Enlightenment thinkers challenged traditional political authority in the 18th century.

parts.label: c
parts.prompt: Explain ONE way European rulers responded to Enlightenment ideas in the 18th century.

rubric.description: E.g., heliocentrism replaced the geocentric model; Newton's universal laws; reliance on observation and experiment over ancient authority.
E.g., Locke's consent and right of revolution; Montesquieu's separation of powers; Rousseau's popular sovereignty; Voltaire's criticism of clerical power.
E.g., enlightened absolutists (Frederick II toleration, Joseph II abolishing serfdom, Catherine II's legal commission); censorship or suppression; limits after Pugachev.

practice.sampleResponse:
(a) Copernicus, Kepler, and Galileo replaced the long-held geocentric model with a heliocentric one, and Newton showed that the same laws of motion and gravitation governed both Earth and the heavens, encouraging Europeans to see nature as orderly and knowable through reason and observation.

(b) John Locke argued that legitimate government rests on the consent of the governed and that people may overthrow rulers who violate their natural rights, directly challenging divine-right claims of absolute monarchs.

(c) Joseph II of Austria responded by implementing reforms inspired by the Enlightenment, such as abolishing serfdom and granting religious toleration, while still ruling as an absolute monarch.
